summary: This document specifies using TLS 1.3 to secure the connection between a TACACS+ client and server. TACACS+ is a protocol for authentication, authorization and accounting on network devices, and its original design had weak protection of its traffic. It updates RFC 8907.

plainLanguage.summary: TACACS+ is the protocol a router uses to ask a central server whether an administrator may log in and what they may do. The old version of the protocol does not really protect that conversation: its built-in scrambling is weak and its shared secret is not a proper authentication. This document puts the whole exchange inside a TLS 1.3 connection, so the traffic is encrypted and both ends prove who they are.

questions: which port does tacacs+ over tls use
subtitle: Putting TACACS+ inside a TLS 1.3 connection so device-admin traffic is really encrypted.

tldr.problem: TACACS+ carries the credentials that let an administrator log into a router or a network access server, and the protocol has no real confidentiality, integrity or authentication of the connection itself. Its obfuscation mechanism uses MD5 and is not encryption.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9887 puts the TACACS+ protocol inside a TLS 1.3 connection, with mutual authentication by certificate. The TLS handshake starts as soon as the TCP connection is up, all TACACS+ messages travel as TLS application data, and the obfuscation option is removed.
tldr.outcome: The document updates RFC 8907, assigns the well-known TCP port 300 for TACACS+ over TLS and keeps port 49 for the older form, and forbids a client from falling back to a non-TLS connection. Sending data before the handshake completes is also forbidden, because TACACS+ data is too sensitive to risk a replay.

today: RFC 9887 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2025, and it has not been obsoleted. It updates RFC 8907 and obsoletes the TACACS+ obfuscation mechanism. IANA has allocated the well-known TCP port 300 under the service name tacacss for TLS-protected TACACS+, while port 49 remains the default for the older unprotected form.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus protocol in RFC 8907 provides device administration for routers, network access servers and other networked computing devices through one or more centralized TACACS+ servers. The protocol provides authentication, authorization and accounting services for TACACS+ clients within the device administration use case.

The content of the protocol is highly sensitive and requires secure transport to safeguard a deployment. However, TACACS+ lacks effective confidentiality, integrity and authentication of the connection and of the network traffic between the TACACS+ server and client, and the security mechanisms described in Section 4.5 of RFC 8907 are extremely weak.

To address these deficiencies, this document updates the TACACS+ protocol to use TLS 1.3 authentication and encryption, and obsoletes the use of TACACS+ obfuscation mechanisms. The maturity of TLS in version 1.3 and above makes it a suitable choice for the TACACS+ protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: TACACS+ is how a router checks with a central server whether a person may log in, what they may do, and how to bill for it. The conversation carries passwords and permissions, so it has to be protected. The original protocol has no real protection, and the scrambling it does have is described in its own specification as obfuscation rather than encryption.

sections.title: TACACS+ over TLS
sections.content:
TACACS+ over TLS takes the protocol defined in RFC 8907, removes the option for obfuscation, and specifies that TLS 1.3 be used for transport. A new well-known default host port number is used.

TLS is introduced into TACACS+ to fulfil two requirements. The first is confidentiality and integrity: the MD5 algorithm underlying the obfuscation mechanism in RFC 8907 has been shown to be insecure when used for encryption, which prevents TACACS+ from being used in a deployment compliant with FIPS 140-3, and securing the protocol with TLS is intended to provide confidentiality and integrity without requiring a secured network. The second is peer authentication: the authentication capabilities of TLS replace the shared secrets of obfuscation for mutual authentication.

Peers implementing this variant must apply mutual authentication and encrypt all data exchanged between them. When the TCP connection is established for the service, a TLS handshake therefore begins immediately. Options that upgrade an initial non-TLS connection must not be used.

To keep TLS traffic clearly separate from traffic without TLS, servers supporting TACACS+ over TLS must listen on a TCP/IP port distinct from the one used by non-TLS TACACS+ servers, and it is further recommended to deploy the TLS and non-TLS services on separate hosts. Given the prevalence of default port usage in existing TACACS+ client implementations, this specification assigns the well-known TCP port number 300 for TACACS+ over TLS. While the designated port is strongly encouraged, deployments with specific requirements may use alternative port numbers, in which case operators must consider the operational implications.
sections.plainLanguage: The change is simple in outline: the TACACS+ messages travel inside TLS instead of travelling in the clear. Because the client cannot tell at the start whether it is talking to a protected or an unprotected service, the two must be told apart by the port number, and the port number for the protected form is 300 rather than 49. A client must not start unprotected and upgrade later, because an attacker could interfere with the upgrade.

sections.title: The TLS Connection
sections.content:
A TACACS+ client initiates a TLS connection by making a TCP connection to a configured TLS TACACS+ server on the TACACS+ TLS port number. Once the TCP connection is established, the client must immediately begin the TLS negotiation before sending any TACACS+ protocol data.

A minimum of TLS 1.3 must be used for transport. It is expected that TACACS+ as described in this document will work with future versions of TLS, but earlier versions of TLS must not be used.

Once the TLS connection has been successfully established, the exchange of TACACS+ data proceeds in accordance with the procedures of RFC 8907. However, all TACACS+ messages must be transmitted as TLS application data, and the TACACS+ obfuscation mechanism must not be applied when operating over TLS.

TLS TACACS+ connections are generally not long-lived. The connection is closed by either peer if it encounters an error or an inactivity timeout. For connections not operating in Single Connection Mode, the TCP session must be closed upon completion of the associated TACACS+ session. Connections in Single Connection Mode may persist for longer but are typically subject to timeout and closure after a brief period of inactivity, so support for transport-layer keepalive mechanisms is not required. Why a connection is closed has no bearing on TLS resumption, unless it was closed by a TLS error, in which case it is possible that the ticket has been invalidated. TACACS+ clients and servers widely support IPv6 configuration in addition to IPv4, and this document makes no changes to the recommendations in that area.
sections.plainLanguage: The client opens a TCP connection to the protected port and starts the TLS handshake at once, before sending anything else. Only TLS 1.3 or later is acceptable. Once the handshake succeeds, the TACACS+ messages are sent as ordinary encrypted application data, and the old scrambling is not applied. These connections are short-lived, so there is no need for keepalive machinery.

sections.title: TLS Authentication Options
sections.content:
Implementations must support certificate-based mutual authentication, to provide a core option for interoperability between deployments. In addition to certificate-based TLS authentication, implementations may support two alternative mechanisms. The first is Pre-Shared Keys, known as external PSKs in TLS 1.3. The second is Raw Public Keys, whose details are considered out of scope for this document.

Certificate-based authentication is the primary option. Deploying it correctly considerably improves the security of a TACACS+ deployment, and it is essential for implementers and operators to understand the implications of a certificate-based solution, including the correct handling of certificates, certificate authorities and all elements of TLS configuration.

Each peer must validate the certificate path of its remote peer, including revocation checking. If verification succeeds, the authentication is successful and the connection is permitted, and policy may impose further constraints on the peer, allowing or denying the connection based on certificate fields or other parameters. Unless disabled by configuration, a peer must not permit the connection of any peer that presents an invalid TLS certificate.

The implementation of certificate-based mutual authentication must support certificate path validation as described in Section 6 of RFC 5280. In some deployments a peer may be isolated from a remote peer's certificate authority, so implementations for these deployments must support certificate chains, where the entire chain of the remote peer's certificate is stored locally. The TLS Cached Information Extension should be implemented, and other approaches for loading intermediate certificates onto the client must include support for revocation checking.
sections.plainLanguage: Both ends must present a certificate and check the other's, down to the certificate authority that issued it, including checking whether it has been revoked. A peer that presents a certificate that does not check out is refused. Where a site cannot reach the certificate authority, the whole chain can be stored on the device instead.

sections.title: Pre-Shared Keys and Resumption
sections.content:
As an alternative to certificate-based authentication, implementations may support PSKs, also known as external PSKs in TLS 1.3. These should not be confused with resumption PSKs. The use of external PSKs is less well established than certificate-based authentication, and it is recommended that systems follow the directions of RFC 9257. Where PSK authentication is implemented, PSK lengths of at least 16 octets must be supported, and the PSK identity must follow the recommendations of Section 6.1 of that document, with implementations supporting PSK identities of at least 16 octets.

Although this document removes the option of obfuscation, it is still possible that the TLS and non-TLS versions of TACACS+ exist in an organisation, for example during migration. In such cases, the shared secrets configured for TACACS+ obfuscation clients must not be the same as the PSKs configured for TLS clients.

TLS resumption can minimize the number of round trips required during the handshake. If a TLS client holds a ticket previously extracted from a NewSessionTicket message from the TLS TACACS+ server, it can use the PSK identity tied to that ticket. If the server consents, the resumed session is acknowledged as authenticated and securely linked to the initial session. The client should use resumption when it holds a valid unused ticket, as each ticket is intended for a single use and is refreshed during resumption. The server can reject a resumption request, but should allow it if the ticket has not expired and has not been used before. When a resumption request arrives, the server may still require a full handshake, in which case the negotiation proceeds as if the session were new.

Because reuse of a ticket allows passive observers to correlate different connections, clients and servers should follow the client tracking preventions of Appendix C.4 of RFC 8446. When processing TLS resumption, certificates must be verified to check for revocation during the period since the last NewSessionTicket message. The resumption ticket lifetime should be configurable, including a zero-seconds lifetime.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of certificates, a pair of endpoints could share a secret in advance, but that option is optional and the secret must be at least 16 bytes long, with an identity of at least 16 bytes as well. The old obfuscation secret must not be reused as the new secret. A client may also keep the ticket the server issued and use it to shorten the next handshake, and the server may refuse that and start again from scratch.

sections.title: Obsolescence of TACACS+ Obfuscation
sections.content:
The obfuscation mechanism documented in Section 4.5 of RFC 8907 is weak. The introduction of TLS authentication and encryption to TACACS+ replaces that mechanism, so obfuscation is hereby obsoleted. This section describes how TACACS+ clients and servers must operate regarding it.

Peers must not use obfuscation with TLS. A TACACS+ client initiating a TLS connection must set the TAC_PLUS_UNENCRYPTED_FLAG bit, thereby asserting that obfuscation is not used for the session, and all subsequent packets must have that bit set to 1.

A TLS TACACS+ server that receives a packet with the TAC_PLUS_UNENCRYPTED_FLAG bit not set to 1 over a TLS connection must return an error of TAC_PLUS_AUTHEN_STATUS_ERROR, TAC_PLUS_AUTHOR_STATUS_ERROR or TAC_PLUS_ACCT_STATUS_ERROR as appropriate for the message type, with the TAC_PLUS_UNENCRYPTED_FLAG bit set to 1, and must terminate the session. A TACACS+ client that receives a packet with the bit not set to 1 must terminate the session and should log the error.
sections.plainLanguage: The old scrambling is withdrawn. Each message on a protected connection carries a flag saying that the old scrambling is not in use, and both ends must set that flag. If a message arrives without it, the session is ended, because that means the other end believes the conversation is still being scrambled.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This document improves the confidentiality, integrity and authentication of the connection and of the network traffic between TACACS+ peers by adding TLS support. Simply adding TLS support does not guarantee the protection of the server and clients, and operators and vendors must adhere to the latest best practices for the integrity of network devices and for selecting secure TLS key and encryption algorithms. The recommendations of BCP 195 must be followed, and any recommendation referring to TLS 1.2 is not relevant here, because TLS 1.3 or above is mandated.

New production deployments should use TLS authentication and encryption. TLS TACACS+ servers must not allow non-TLS connections, because of the threat of downgrade attacks or misconfiguration, and separate non-TLS servers should be set up for the clients that need them. It is not recommended that TLS and non-TLS TACACS+ servers be deployed on the same host. TACACS+ clients must not fall back to a non-TLS connection if a TLS connection fails, and that prohibition includes the period during a migration.

On early data, TLS 1.3 resumption and PSK techniques make it possible to send data before the handshake completes, which carries a replay risk. Given the sensitivity of TACACS+ data, clients must not send data until the full handshake completes, and TLS TACACS+ servers must abruptly disconnect clients that do. Clients and servers must not include the early_data extension.

Operators should be aware that the SNI extension is part of the TLS client hello, which is sent in cleartext and is therefore subject to eavesdropping. Operators should also be aware of the risk of isolation from a peer's certificate authority by network failure, which causes certificate verification, and therefore peer authentication, to fail; storing the chain locally can help.

The use of wildcards in TLS server identities creates a single point of failure, because a compromised private key of a wildcard certificate affects every server using it. Operators must ensure that the wildcard is limited to a subdomain dedicated solely to TLS TACACS+ servers, and that the servers covered by the wildcard certificate are impervious to redirection of traffic to a different server.

On the port number, a new port is considered appropriate rather than a mechanism that negotiates an upgrade from an initial non-TLS connection, because it allows the unobfuscated connections to be blocked by port number, leaves passive intrusion detection systems monitoring the unobfuscated form unaffected, avoids on-path attacks that interfere with an upgrade, and prevents the accidental exposure of sensitive information due to misconfiguration. However, the coexistence of the older authentication and obfuscation with the newer one also presents an opportunity for downgrade attacks, for example by causing failures of connections to the TLS-enabled service. The simplest mitigation is to refuse non-TLS connections at the host entirely, perhaps by using separate hosts, and peers should support configuration that requires the use of TLS globally and per peer, with the TLS versions and algorithms offered limited to those recommended by standards bodies.
sections.plainLanguage: Several rules protect the connection. A client that cannot get a protected connection must fail rather than fall back to the unprotected one, since a fall-back is exactly what an attacker wants. Data must not be sent before the handshake finishes, because early data can be replayed. The name of the server travels in cleartext in the client hello, so it is visible to anyone watching. And a certificate with a wildcard covers many servers, so losing its key loses all of them at once, which is why the wildcard should sit in a subdomain used only for these servers.

sections.title: Operational Considerations
sections.content:
It is essential for operators to understand the implications of a certificate-based authentication solution, including the correct handling of certificates, certificate authorities and all elements of TLS configuration, and to provision certificates to all peers, including the TLS clients, so that the mandatory mutual authentication can happen.

The configuration scheme for enabling TLS must be straightforward and must leave no room for ambiguity about whether TLS or non-TLS will be used between a client and a server. This document recommends the use of a separate port number for TLS servers. Where deployments have not overridden the defaults explicitly, client implementations must use port 49 for non-TLS TACACS+ and port 300 for TLS TACACS+. Implementors may offer a single option to disable all non-TLS operations: on a server it then does not respond to any non-TLS client connection, and on a client it never establishes one.

During the migration from a non-TLS deployment, operators may need to support both kinds of server. The migration phase lets a deployment move gradually from an insecure state to a more secure one, but it is vulnerable to downgrade attacks and should be considered insecure until it is fully completed. The period in which any client is configured with both TLS and non-TLS servers should be minimised, and the operator must consider the security impact of supporting both.

Some client devices in a deployment may not implement TLS and will need access to non-TLS servers, so operators should deploy separate non-TLS servers for those clients rather than sharing the hosts used for TLS clients.

On the registry, IANA has allocated the service name tacacss on TCP port 300, described as the TLS Secure Login Host Protocol. The name follows the common practice of appending an s to the name given to the non-TLS well-known port name. Considerations about service discovery are out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: The operational work is mostly about not leaving gaps. Every device that will act as a client needs a certificate, so that both ends of the connection can authenticate. The configuration must make it obvious whether a given server is the protected one, which is why the port number carries that meaning. While old and new servers run side by side during a migration, an attacker can still push traffic onto the old path, so that period should be as short as possible.
